# 2026-11-21: How information spreads along a chain {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
**Status:** promoted to @sec-push and @sec-chains · **Thread:** T2 · **Checked by:** `tests/test_chain.py`
:::

**Question.** The [note on propagation](2026-11-21-information-propagation.qmd) showed
that a part of the body holds the contact force through an effective contact damping
$b_{\rm eff}(\omega)\ge b_c$, raised by the internal dampers. On the SEA there is one
internal damper and two parts. What happens in a body with many dampers between the
contact and a part, such as a chain of masses or a rod?

**Findings.** Shake the body at the part. Each internal damper then adds its damping
times the square of its stretch per unit motion of the contact point to $b_{\rm eff}$.
This follows from reciprocity and holds for any linear body with symmetric mass,
stiffness and damping. In a chain, the cost of a
damper between the contact and the part is the same for every part beyond it, so these
costs only accumulate with distance. Dampers beyond the part add a second cost, which
we call backflow. At low frequency backflow vanishes and each damper on the way costs
$b_j(k_c/k_j)^2$, where $k_c$ is the contact stiffness and $k_j$ the damper's spring.
Information therefore crosses a stiff interior well and a soft one badly. In band, the
backflow can dominate: on a rod the contact point itself holds the least, because it
loses near the natural frequencies of the body held fixed at the contact.

**Where it lives now.** The definitions, proofs, figures and numbers moved to @sec-push and @sec-chains of
the chapter on information inside the body. This note keeps the dated record of the
question and what was found.
